keyVerseText: Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?
rootMeaning: The Greek word λεγεών (legeṓn) originates from the Latin term legio, referring to a Roman military regiment. This etymology highlights its literal sense as a large, organized body of soldiers. Beyond the common English translation 'legion,' the root meaning emphasizes the concept of strength, order, and formidable power inherent in a disciplined military unit.
usageInScripture: The term λεγεών appears four times in the New Testament, consistently referring to either a legion of soldiers or figuratively to a vast number of spiritual beings, such as angels or demons. Its translations include 'legions,' 'is Legion,' 'the legion,' and 'Legion,' showing a consistent reference to a large, powerful group. This uniformity in usage underscores its association with overwhelming force or multitude.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding λεγεών as a term denoting a powerful, organized force enriches our grasp of spiritual realities portrayed in Scripture. It reminds believers of the vastness and strength of God's heavenly hosts as well as the formidable opposition posed by demonic forces. This word points to the sovereignty of Christ who, by His authority, can command legions of angels, demonstrating His supreme power over both the seen and unseen realms. In the Christian faith, it reassures believers that no earthly or spiritual army can thwart God's divine purposes.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 26:53, Jesus declares, 'Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?' Here, λεγεών conveys the immense and organized power at God's disposal, far exceeding human military might. This highlights Christ's divine authority and the assurance that His mission is undergirded by heavenly strength, even though He chooses the path of humility and submission. The word deepens the reader's appreciation of the spiritual resources available to Jesus in His redemptive work.
